title: Utilise growth media for ornamental plant containers

lessons.title: What growing media is made of
lessons.html:
What is a growing medium?

Plants in pots and bags cannot send roots deep into the ground. They live in a small amount of soil-like mix. This mix is called a growing medium. It must hold the plant up, keep water, let air in and give food.

Common parts of a growing medium

PartWhat it does
Composted pine barkMain base in many SA nurseries. Light, holds some water, drains well.
Coir (coconut fibre)Holds water well. Used instead of peat.
PeatHolds a lot of water. Often imported and expensive.
CompostAdds food and life. Must be well rotted.
River sandMakes the mix heavier and helps drainage.
PerliteWhite, light stones. Add air spaces.
VermiculiteShiny, light flakes. Hold water and food.
Garden soil (topsoil)Sometimes added, but can bring weeds, pests and disease.

Other things that may be added

  • Fertiliser, often slow-release granules
  • Lime, to change how sour (acid) the mix is
  • Water-holding crystals, in some mixes

Telling them apart

Your supervisor will show you each one. Feel it in your hand. Look at the colour. Bark is brown and chunky. Coir is brown and stringy. Perlite is white and very light. Sand is gritty. Learn the names and where each bag is kept in the store.

Safety

  • Wear gloves. Compost and bark can have germs, and bark has splinters.
  • Wear a dust mask when working with dry perlite, vermiculite or peat. Do not breathe the dust.
  • Lift bags with your knees bent and back straight. Get help for heavy bags.
  • Wash your hands before you eat.

lessons.title: Porosity: air and water in the mix
lessons.html:
Roots need air and water

Roots need water to drink and air to breathe. In a pot, the spaces between the pieces of mix hold the air and water. These spaces are called pores. Porosity means how much space there is in the mix.

  • Big pores let water drain out and air come in.
  • Small pores hold water for the plant.

A good mix has both.

What happens with the wrong mix

MixProblem
Too fine, like clay or fine soilStays wet. No air. Roots rot. Leaves turn yellow.
Too coarse, like big bark chunks onlyDries out fast. Plant wilts. Needs water all the time.

A simple test you can do

  1. Take a pot with holes in the bottom and close the holes with tape.
  2. Fill the pot with the mix.
  3. Slowly pour in water from a measuring jug until the water reaches the top of the mix. Write down how much water you used.
  4. Hold the pot over an empty jug and take off the tape. Let the water run out.
  5. Measure the water that came out.

A lot of water in the mix means the mix has many pores. The water that runs out shows the big air pores. The water that stays in shows how much water the mix holds. Compare two or three mixes and talk about the results with your supervisor.

Feeling the mix

Squeeze a handful of damp mix. A good mix holds together a little, then breaks apart when you touch it. If water drips out, it is too wet. If it falls apart like dust, it is too dry or too coarse.

Different plants like different mixes. Succulents and aloes like a mix that drains fast. Ferns like a mix that holds more water.

lessons.title: Blending and mixing growing media
lessons.html:
Blending: choosing the amounts

Blending means deciding how much of each part goes in. The nursery has a recipe. For example, a recipe could be 3 buckets of bark, 1 bucket of coir and 1 bucket of perlite. Always follow the recipe your supervisor gives you. Use the same bucket or wheelbarrow to measure every part, so the amounts stay right.

Mixing by hand

  1. Choose a clean, hard surface, like a concrete slab, or a clean mixing tray.
  2. Put on gloves and a dust mask.
  3. Measure each part and pour it in a heap.
  4. Wet dry parts like coir or peat a little first. Dry mix is dusty and does not mix well.
  5. Add fertiliser or lime by spreading it thinly over the heap, as the recipe says.
  6. Turn the heap with a spade from one side to the other. Do this at least three times.
  7. Check that the colour looks the same all through. No lumps, no pockets of one part.

Mixing with a machine

Some nurseries use a cement mixer or a special media mixer. Only use it if you are trained. Keep hands, spades and loose clothing out of the moving drum. Switch it off before you reach in.

Storing the mix

  • Cover the mix so rain does not wash it and weeds do not blow in.
  • Keep it off the ground on a slab, so soil and germs do not get in.
  • Label the heap or bags with the name of the mix and the date.
  • Use mix with fertiliser soon. Old mix with fertiliser can burn roots.

Cleaning up

Sweep up spilled mix, clean the tools and put bags back in the store. Wash your hands.

Key points

  • Know the parts: bark, coir, compost, sand, perlite and vermiculite.
  • Roots need both air and water; porosity is the space for them.
  • Follow the recipe and measure with the same container.
  • Mix until the colour is even, and wear gloves and a dust mask.
  • Cover and label stored mix.
